claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a continuous fcc matrix containing dispersed C14 Laves-phase precipitates.
The C14 Laves phase is enriched in Ti and likely contains Fe and Ni.
Strong antiferromagnetic coupling occurs between fcc Fe-Co-Ni sublattices and Ti-enriched regions of the C14 phase.
Ti is non-magnetic in the relevant FeCoNiTi microstructure.
Ti in the C14 phase modifies the local electronic environment and polarizes the adjacent fcc phase.
The interfacial polarization produces a magnetic dead layer or reduced moment at the fcc/C14 interface.
Antiferromagnetic interfacial coupling suppresses the saturation magnetization of the fcc phase by partially canceling ferromagnetic alignment.
The C14 phase pins magnetic domain walls because of magnetic-anisotropy contrast and lattice mismatch at fcc/C14 interfaces.
Strain fields around C14 precipitates and antiferromagnetic coupling increase the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
Microstructural decomposition and incorporation of an antiferromagnetic constituent can coincide with reduced saturation magnetization and increased coercivity in a high-entropy alloy.
The proposed interfacial coupling and pinning mechanism produces a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because their orbital moments are insufficient to generate high anisotropy.
The transition near 1084 K corresponds to magnetic ordering of the fcc phase.
The transition near 214 K marks the onset of antiferromagnetic interfacial coupling.
The transition near 168 K corresponds to ordering of the C14 phase.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization at 400 K than a single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi alloy.
The proposed mechanism may cease to operate if C14 is absent, its phase fraction is too low, or Ti content is insufficient.
DFT calculations comparing an fcc model with and without a Ti-rich C14 interface can test the spin-resolved density of states at the Fermi level and interphase exchange coupling.
Adjusting Ti content or heat treatment can produce a suitable single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi control by dissolving the C14 phase.

contradictions.description: Ti is described as non-magnetic, while the coupling is repeatedly phrased as antiferromagnetic coupling between magnetic transition-metal sublattices and Ti-enriched regions. This can be coherent if Ti only mediates coupling, but the hypothesis does not clearly distinguish Ti-mediated exchange from a magnetic Ti sublattice.

The proposed decisive electronic criterion is a reduction in spin density of states at the Fermi level, whereas the predicted outcome concerns reduced saturation magnetization. These quantities are not equivalent, so absence of an SDOS reduction would not by itself decisively falsify the stated moment-cancellation mechanism.
